claims.claim: Lakehouse Tables holds managed Delta tables and Files holds unstructured or non-Delta data; only Delta tables appear in the SQL analytics endpoint; default semantic models are no longer created automatically since 5 September 2025.
Non-Delta folders under Tables and broken shortcuts appear in the Unidentified area.
Schemas are enabled by default for new lakehouses; dbo cannot be renamed or removed; Spark uses workspace.lakehouse.schema.table and resolves omitted parts from defaults.

concept_html:
A lakehouse has two top-level areas in OneLake:

  • Tables holds managed Delta tables. Fabric registers them, the SQL analytics endpoint exposes them, and Direct Lake semantic models read them.
  • Files holds anything else: CSV, JSON, Parquet, images, raw deliveries.

Only Delta tables in Tables reach the SQL engines. A Parquet or CSV file is invisible to the SQL analytics endpoint, wherever it sits. If you put a folder that is not a valid Delta table under Tables, the lakehouse explorer shows it in an Unidentified area. A broken shortcut also lands there.

So the flow for a delivery is: land the raw file in Files (your bronze copy, as received), then read it with Spark and write a Delta table to Tables with saveAsTable.

Schemas. New lakehouses created in the portal have schemas enabled by default. Every schema-enabled lakehouse has a dbo schema that you cannot rename or remove. A table written without a schema goes to dbo. Create schemas by domain (sales, hr) to keep a growing lakehouse navigable.

In Spark SQL you reference tables with a four-part name: workspace.lakehouse.schema.table. Parts you leave out come from defaults: a bare table name means the dbo schema of the notebook's default lakehouse. For code that others run, name at least the lakehouse and schema, so it does not depend on which lakehouse happens to be attached.

One change to note if you learned Fabric earlier: since 5 September 2025, Fabric no longer creates a default semantic model automatically with each new lakehouse. Create semantic models on purpose (lesson C6-L1).

lines: from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import types as T
RESPONDENT_SCHEMA = T.StructType([
T.StructField("respondent_id", T.StringType(), False),
T.StructField("wave", T.IntegerType(), False),
T.StructField("weight", T.DoubleType(), True),
])
def load_delivery(spark: SparkSession, path: str, table: str) -> DataFrame:
"""Read a CSV delivery from Files and append it to a managed Delta table in Tables."""
df = spark.read.option("header", True).schema(RESPONDENT_SCHEMA).csv(path)
df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable(table)
return df
load_delivery(spark, "Files/landing/respondents_w14.csv", "lh_survey.sales.respondents")

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import types as T

RESPONDENT_SCHEMA = T.StructType([
    T.StructField("respondent_id", T.StringType(), False),
    T.StructField("wave", T.IntegerType(), False),
    T.StructField("weight", T.DoubleType(), True),
])


def load_delivery(spark: SparkSession, path: str, table: str) -> DataFrame:
    """Read a CSV delivery and append it to a managed Delta table.

    Args:
        spark: Active session.
        path: CSV path, usually under Files/landing.
        table: Target table, ideally lakehouse.schema.table.

    Returns:
        The DataFrame that was read.
    """
    df = spark.read.option("header", True).schema(RESPONDENT_SCHEMA).csv(path)
    df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable(table)
    return df

title: Lakehouse Tables and Files, and schemas
why_html: An engineer wrote cleaned survey data as Parquet into Files/clean/respondents/, the way they had written to cloud storage before. The Power BI team could not find the table in the SQL analytics endpoint, so they imported the Parquet into a separate dataflow, a second copy with its own refresh. Writing a Delta table to Tables with saveAsTable would have exposed it to every engine with no copy.
